analysis.one_liner: Bars states and cities from regulating rifles and shotguns more strictly than federal law.
analysis.headline: Introduced by Rep. Elise Stefanik with 6 Republican cosponsors on March 9, 2021, referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then its crime subcommittee in May 2021, and never received a committee or floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The SAGA Act would amend federal criminal law so that no state or local government could impose any rule on rifles or shotguns — including their parts, detachable magazines, and pistol-grip or stock designs — that is stricter than federal law, or charge any tax or fee on them above the federal amount. Any state or local law that conflicts, including laws already on the books, would have no force or effect, and anyone who wins a lawsuit over this could collect attorney's fees from the government. Because federal law requires no license to own most rifles and shotguns, this would wipe out state assault-weapon bans, large-capacity magazine limits, and state registration and licensing systems.
analysis.who_benefits: Gun owners in states with strict firearm laws, who could buy, sell, and possess rifles, shotguns, magazines, and features their states currently restrict. Firearm and magazine manufacturers and dealers would gain the most in practical terms: a uniform national market with the country's stricter state laws — New York's, California's, New Jersey's, Massachusetts's — voided overnight.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gun owners and firearm makers in strict states

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits any state or local regulation, prohibition, or registration or licensing requirement on rifles or shotguns — including parts, detachable magazines, and grip or stock designs — that is more restrictive than federal law, and voids any conflicting state or local law whether passed before or after enactment.
Bars states and localities from imposing any penalty, tax, fee, or charge on rifles or shotguns greater than what federal law provides.
Gives prevailing plaintiffs in lawsuits over these restrictions a court-ordered award of attorney's fees on top of any damages, making it cheaper to challenge state gun laws.

analysis.who_pays: State and local governments, which would lose their authority over rifles and shotguns within their borders and would face lawsuits with fee-shifting. Communities that rely on stricter state gun laws — including police departments that use state licensing and registration systems for investigations — would bear the public-safety consequences supporters of those laws point to.

drawbacks.text: It would void state laws enacted before the bill's passage, immediately overturning existing assault-weapon bans, magazine limits, and registration or licensing requirements in restrictive states rather than only blocking future ones.
Because federal law sets no license or registration requirement for owning most rifles and shotguns, the 'no stricter than federal' floor is very low — nearly any state rule in this space would fall.
The attorney-fee provision would push state and local governments to defend themselves in court against suits over their own gun laws, adding taxpayer legal costs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivers a clear, immediate benefit to gun owners in states with strict firearm laws and a large commercial benefit to the firearm and ammunition industry, while stripping states of a police power they have used for decades and inviting litigation against them. Whether that trade favors ordinary people depends on where you stand on gun regulation itself; the bill does not attempt to balance the two — it simply nationalizes the most permissive standard for rifles and shotguns.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, then to its crime subcommittee in May 2021, and never received a markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Elise Stefanik introduced the bill on March 9, 2021, joined by six Republican cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced.
On May 18, 2021, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security, and no further action was taken for the rest of the Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State and local governments kept their existing rifle and shotgun laws, and firearm manufacturers gained nothing they did not already have. Gun owners in restrictive states saw no change either way.

for.name: Rep. Elise Stefanik
for.role: Sponsor, House Representative from New York
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited six cosponsors.

against.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee action; it remained in subcommittee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 6 cosponsors were Republicans; the bill died in the Democratic-controlled House Judiciary Committee without a vote, so no roll calls ever split on it.

industries.industry: Firearm and magazine manufacturers and retailers
industries.note: The bill would void every state ban or limit stricter than federal law — including rules on assault-style rifles, large-capacity magazines, and registration — giving the industry a uniform national market overnight. The industry's gain comes directly from knocking down the state restrictions gun-regulation supporters consider public-safety measures, so its interest runs against those residents' wishes.

They would lose all authority to regulate rifles and shotguns beyond the federal floor and would owe attorney's fees when gun-rights plaintiffs win challenges to their laws. Their regulatory authority is the mechanism their residents use to set local gun rules.
